 Flix OM review: Dhanush and Mammootty team up for a spy thriller that loses the plot halfway 
 Dhanush and Mammootty’s ‘Operation Mole’ works best in the first half, leading up to an emotional interval sequence. It just feels as if the film lost interest in itself after the break and tried to make up for it with increasingly convenient twists and long fight sequences. Written by: Bharathy Singaravel Published on :  20 Nov 2026, 1:26 pm 
 Copied 
 OM: Operation Mole (Tamil)   
 In 2015, the Andhra Pradesh Red Sanders Anti-Smuggling Task Force opened fire on 20 Tamil labourers in Seshachalam. The cops claimed it was self-defence. The men’s families and human rights organisations have maintained that these were unprovoked extrajudicial murders. 
 At the time, police said they stumbled on the men attempting to cut down red sanders trees for smuggling. But allegations only grew that the so-called ‘encounter’ was staged. No clear answers have emerged since. 
 Their deaths are the heart of Director Rajkumar Periasamy’s OM: Operation Mole. Dhanush plays Palani alias Thirukumaran, a special operative trained in infiltrating organised crime networks. He’s soon sent undercover to a Red Sanders smuggling operation. Here, Palani meets Karthikeyan (Mammootty), who oversees the Chennai arm of the network. 
 Karthikeyan, like Mammootty in the 1991 Thalapathi , is a gangster well-loved by his neighbourhood. He has his own codes and is mindful of who is most vulnerable to the ongoing feud between smugglers and cops. He values loyalty above all else. As Palani and Karthikeyan grow closer, OM makes some vague attempts to recall the bond between Devaraj (Mammootty) and Surya (Rajinikanth) in Thalapathi but isn’t too serious about it. 
 Palani’s handler is Nithya Reddy (Sai Pallavi), who heads the AP task force. She has personal as well as professional reasons to stop the smuggling network. 
 Soon, Palani makes himself Karthikeyan’s most trusted worker and surrogate son. Using this leverage, Nithya makes plans to bring in the network’s entire high command, including a mysterious boss known only as Abdul Hamid (Naseeruddin Shah). Shah is criminally wasted in his role. 
 Even the best-laid plans need convoluted Kollywood plot twists, however. 
 The Seshachalam extrajudicial killings, or an event closely based on it, down to the year and region, upset events on both sides. Palani, who is already battling with his affection for Karthikeyan, is left hollowed out and derailed. 
 Suddenly, the binary of heroes and villains blurs for him. Nithya too is horrified. Yet she remains undeterred, setting up conflict between her and Palani. 
 The first half closes with a whirlwind of moving chess pieces and complex moral questions. Despite the overly convenient twists, OM keeps you hooked until the interval. 
 Then comes a second half that wants to do and say too much with the remaining 1 hour 30 minutes. How much can the film authentically probe police brutality? OM can’t decide.
 It raises pertinent questions such as asking who gets killed off in ‘encounters’ and who gets a chance to plead their case legally. But it quickly finds inane arguments to refute exactly that. 
 The vulnerability of Adivasi communities to police overreach is highlighted and again undercut by highly sentimentalised victim blaming and saviour tropes. Any real confrontation between state authorities and the families of victims of extrajudicial killings is swiftly taken off camera. Dhanush has done all the talking required that the audiences need to listen to. 
 What kind of political impact OM, with its Chandrababu Naidu look-alike Andhra chief minister, may achieve remains to be seen. It is appreciable that the film has brought the Seshachalam killings back into the limelight. But it also takes care to present the issue as the work of a few bad apples rather than the result of systemic police overreach. How much does such a narrative truly benefit the victims of state violence?
 While the second half fractalises in many directions, it is OM ’s stars who keep you caring at all. 
 Sai Pallavi is brilliant and a constant joy to watch. She flows effortlessly between Tamil, Telugu and English dialogues, never losing momentum or gravitas. Whether faced with moral ambiguity on the job or engaged in fight sequences alongside Dhanush and Mammootty, she is flawless. 
 Next to her, Dhanush comes across as unexceptional. His performance is solid and hard to fault. Yet, it’s barely a role that’ll stay with you like his characters in Vada Chennai (2018), Asuran (2019) or Karnan (2021). It’s really Palani’s relationship with Karthikeyan that makes his role work. 
 Karthikeyan, while bafflingly too trusting for a crime boss, is the most human when he has to accept who Palani really is. He is hurt; he grieves. But never does he have a moment of rage at the betrayal. He meets this pain with the world-weariness of a man who has been fighting for too long. 
 Sreeleela as Palani’s wife, Roja, is the weakest link in the cast. Too often, she is simply too grating. She comes across more as a sulky child than an adult attempting to communicate her anger and needs. 
 OM works best during its first half, leading up to an emotional interval sequence. It just feels as if the film lost interest in itself after the break and tried to make up with increasingly handy twists and prolonged fight sequences.
